g.text: The supplied breach index (xposedornot, retrieved via breach_index) reports that
test@example.com appears in 80 separate breach collections, and all 80 were
enumerated in the returned data. Confirmed findings are limited to appearance of
the address in those collections: every entry carries a null breach date and an
empty data_types list, so neither the exposure date nor the specific fields
exposed can be verified from this data. The pipeline's own signal block records
credential_bearing = 0 while setting risk_floor = high, meaning the high rating
is driven by the breadth of the exposure surface rather than by any confirmed
password or credential leak. It is plausible, but not established here, that
some of these collections (for example Cit0day, Collection-1 and OGusers-2020,
which are aggregator or credential-oriented sets) contain password material;
that remains an inference until data types are confirmed. No associated
accounts, handles, or hostnames were returned by any source, so the account and
subdomain sections are empty rather than negative findings.
Only one source was queried: breach_index (backed by xposedornot). It returned
unavailable_sources is empty, so no source is known to have failed or been
The source reported breach_count = 80 and enumerated all 80 entries; no
truncation of the source list occurred. The 15 entries above were selected for
consumer platforms), not by date, because no dates were supplied.
Every returned breach record has date = null and data_types = []. Absence of
data types is a reporting gap in the source, not evidence that only
The signal block states credential_bearing = 0 while risk_floor = high; these
are consistent only if the high floor is derived from breach volume rather than
No account handles, profile URLs, or subdomains were returned by any source;
the associated_accounts and subdomains sections are empty because nothing was
found, not because those checks were performed and cleared.
No verification of breach authenticity, deduplication across collections, or
recency weighting was possible from the supplied data.
Treat the address as widely circulated: assume it is on credential-stuffing
lists and stop using it as a login identifier for any account that matters.
Change the password on every account registered to test@example.com, starting
with the platforms named above (LinkedIn, Twitter, Patreon, Chegg, SoundCloud,
Last.fm, Roblox), and set a unique password per site via a password manager.
Enable phishing-resistant MFA (passkey or hardware key, then TOTP app) on
those accounts; do not rely on SMS where another factor is offered.
Query each named platform's own account-recovery or 'download your data' flow
to confirm whether an account actually exists for this address before acting on
it, since the index does not prove account existence.
Re-run the breach lookup against a source that returns breach dates and data
types (for example HIBP with the unverified/verified flags shown) so the 80 hits
can be dated and the credential-bearing subset identified.
Set up a monitoring alert for this address and for any alias you migrate to,
and retire the address from public-facing use where possible.
If this address was used for financial or crypto services (the index lists
Coinmama, Betterment, Ameriprise), review those statements and login history
directly with the provider rather than relying on the index.
